Ex-Sweden air cargo rates ease to SAfrica, Japan
By Abigail Schmelz

STOCKHOLM, Oct 9 (Reuter) - Air cargo rates from Stockholm to Johannesburg and Tokyo eased over the past month as a smattering of new cargo capacity hit the market, a Reuter survey of airlines and freight forwarders showed.
Market players agreed traffic volumes had picked up, but some said it was a typical autumn rush while others said it was unusually busy.
"We are awaiting the expected autumn boom. There's an upward trend in general for the export market. We are beginning to notice this now," Lufthansa Cargo regional director Sweden Sven Ahlberg said.
Airlines said traffic volumes has increased, especially to the Far East, but rates were still under pressure.
"Despite the fact there is good demand there is still pressure on rates," said Erik Lundqvist, Scandinavian Airlines System's director of cargo capacity and yield management.

"We're seeing an improvement in September as compared to last year. It's very market specific. I'm seeing a clear improvement to the Far East, but I'm very disappointed with what we're seeing to the North Atlantic."
Lundqvist said rate pressure to New York, Chicago and Seattle -- the North Atlantic -- was due to lower volumes.
But he there was still pressure on rates to the Far East even though demand still exceeded supply.
British Airways World Cargo manager Sweden Anders Uddman said the British carrier was less exposed to Far East spots and the autumn season was no different than last year.
"Business is stable, it's fairly good. Yields are holding up. Noone is making any moves on the market," Uddman said.
"The exports went a bit soft in the beginning of the year, but they seem to have recovered now."
Transatlantic rates were little changed from the last Swedish air cargo market report on August 9, staying at around 9.75 crowns a kg for a 100 kg shipment to New York's JFK.
Average rates to Chicago and Los Angeles were both unchanged at 11.30 and 12.70 crowns per kg respectively.
Analysts said Scandinavian Airlines System's Boeing 747 freighter Gothenburg-New York was still hit by competition from passenger planes vying to fill their cargo holds at cut prices.

Rates to the Far East were steady, with market players reporting cargo traffic volumes busy. The rates to Hong Kong and to Singapore were the same at 13.30 crowns per kg while Bangkok was flat at 13 crowns per kg, unchanged from the August report.
"The market for us to Asia is booming. We've had to turn away bookings due to space limitations," said Singapore Airlines cargo manager for Scandinavia and Finland Jens Heide.
"It's been two years since we've seen a boom like this."
Heide said Chinese destinations such as Guangdong and Shanghai were busiest, followed by Australian cities. He expected the rush to continue at least until year end.
Bengt Lundell, Finnair cargo manager for Sweden, said there was an export boom on long haul traffic to the Far East, especially China, and to the United States.

"I think there will be a shortage of space. All the agents are claiming they have never had so much cargo in one year. It's expanding very rapidly at the moment and we think it will continue until the end of the year," Lundell said.
Rates to Japan eased to 19.30 crowns per kg from 19.40 crowns as the effects of the SAS freighter from Gothenburg to Osaka twice weekly fed into the market.
Rates to Dubai were flat at 10.25 crowns per kg.

The price war for cargo to South Africa hotted up as South African Airways said it planned to start a weekly freight service on October 13 from Johannesburg to Stockholm with an Airbus 300 with a 36 tonne capacity.
The average rate fell to 20.20 crowns per kilo from 20.60.
"I am getting rates below 19 crowns, still with good service," one freight forwarder said.
Some players said the volumes of available shipments did not justify adding capacity.

"Everyone, all of a sudden, seems to be interested in South Africa," said Mikael Adriansson, air cargo manager at Kuhne & Nagel. "The rates are now lower than they have been for 15, 16, or 17 years, evidence that volumes aren't that big."
The rate to London was steady at 7.70 crowns per kg and to Paris it was also unchanged at 7.50 crowns.
The average rate to Sao Paulo was flat at 21.80 crowns.
Players were mixed about the new capacity on the market.
KLM Royal Dutch Airlines was planning to start operating a Shorts Belfast freighter between Amsterdam Schiphol and Stockholm five times weekly on Monday to Friday from October 1.
Lufthansa Cargo increased the frequency of its Boeing 737QC, with a 15-tonne capacity on the Frankfurt-Stockholm-East Midlands-Frankfurt line to five times weekly from four.
"I think the new space will be welcomed," Singapore Airlines' Heide said.

"We see better capacity utilisation with the flight to East Midlands. From last week we increased the frequency from four to five times weekly. We saw already in the first week there was a need for this extra frequency," Lufthansa Cargo's Ahlberg said.
KLM's service seemed to mostly be taking over cargo which had previously been trucked to Amsterdam, said Par Wahlstedt, manager at freight forwarder United Air Service.
"The loser will be the truck driver," Wahlstedt said.

"We are preparing for the end of the year. It is normally very busy for everybody. If there is a shortage of space, it will show now," said Thomas Hancock, central shipping and forwarding manager at Ericsson Radio Systems.
